cards.front: In neuron recordings, what is a burst and what is a pause?
cards.back: A burst is a brief jump in firing rate (spikes per second) above the resting rate. A pause is a brief drop below it.
cards.quote: A burst is a brief jump in a neuron's firing rate (spikes per second) above its resting rate, and a pause is a brief drop below it.
cards.section: Two questions, one idea

cards.front: In the lesson's trained, predictably timed reward tasks, what does the quick burst or pause of many midbrain dopamine neurons report?
cards.back: A reward prediction error: whether things turned out better or worse than predicted, counting both reward that arrives and news of reward to come. At the reward, it is reward received minus reward predicted.
cards.quote: A midbrain dopamine neuron's quick burst or pause reports a reward prediction error: whether things just turned out better or worse than the animal predicted
cards.section: Two questions, one idea

cards.front: What kind of conclusion can each experiment support: a recording, a stimulation, and a silencing or ablation?
cards.back: Recording: correlation (activity goes with an event). Stimulation: sufficiency (imposed activity is enough to produce a behaviour). Silencing or ablation: necessity (the cells are needed for the behaviour).
cards.quote: Both halves of the lesson use three kinds of experiment, and each answers a different question.
cards.section: Two questions, one idea

cards.front: Fat cells make a hormone, {{c1::leptin}}, roughly in proportion to how much fat is stored.
cards.quote: Fat cells make a hormone, leptin, roughly in proportion to how much fat is stored.
cards.section: The picture first: what a fast does

cards.front: During a fast, what happens to blood leptin, and how does that shift arcuate AgRP and POMC neuron activity?
cards.back: Leptin falls. Leptin normally inhibits AgRP neurons and excites POMC neurons, so falling leptin (with other deficit signals) shifts AgRP neurons toward more activity and POMC neurons toward less.
cards.quote: In the arcuate nucleus, at the base of the hypothalamus, leptin normally inhibits AgRP neurons and excites POMC neurons.
cards.section: The picture first: what a fast does

cards.front: POMC neurons make pro-opiomelanocortin, which is cleaved into {{c1::alpha-MSH}}, an MC4R agonist that reduces feeding.
cards.back: AgRP, from AgRP neurons, is an MC4R antagonist.
cards.quote: POMC neurons make pro-opiomelanocortin, which is cleaved into alpha-MSH, an MC4R agonist that reduces feeding
cards.section: The picture first: what a fast does

cards.front: Using MC4R as a 'stop button', explain why a fast raises the drive to eat.
cards.back: POMC neurons press the button (alpha-MSH activates MC4R); AgRP covers it (blocks MC4R). In a fast MC4R gets less alpha-MSH and more AgRP, so the stop signal weakens and the drive to eat rises.
cards.quote: Think of MC4R as a stop button: POMC neurons press it, AgRP covers it.
cards.section: The picture first: what a fast does

cards.front: Leptin replacement reduced ob/ob mouse body weight by 30% after two weeks. Why does it not reliably treat common human obesity?
cards.back: Most people with common obesity already have high leptin, not too little. Replacement worked in leptin-deficient ob/ob mice and in rare people born unable to make leptin, but does not reliably treat common obesity.
cards.why: Leptin acts more like a fuel gauge than a brake; its strongest role is probably signalling starvation when it falls.
cards.quote: Most people with common obesity have high leptin, not too little
cards.section: The picture first: what a fast does

cards.front: What is parabiosis?
cards.back: Surgically joining two animals so they exchange some blood.
cards.quote: He used parabiosis: surgically joining two animals so they exchange some blood.
cards.section: Evidence for a hormone: joined mice

cards.front: An ob/ob mouse (obese, lacks a circulating satiety factor but can respond to it) is joined by parabiosis to a db/db mouse (obese, makes the factor but cannot respond). Predict what happens to the ob/ob mouse, and why.
cards.back: The ob/ob mouse stops eating, loses weight and eventually starves. The db/db partner makes a large amount of the factor, and the ob/ob mouse, which can respond, receives a strong dose.
cards.quote: The ob/ob mouse stopped eating, lost weight and eventually starved.
cards.section: Evidence for a hormone: joined mice

cards.front: What do the mouse ob and db genes encode?
cards.back: ob encodes leptin, a protein of about 16 kDa made by fat. db encodes the leptin receptor, which signals through the JAK-STAT pathway.
cards.quote: The db gene turned out to encode the leptin receptor, which signals through the pathway taught in JAK-STAT signalling.
cards.section: Evidence for a hormone: leptin

cards.front: Daily injections of recombinant leptin are given to ob/ob mice and to db/db mice for two weeks. Predict which strain loses weight, and why.
cards.back: Only the ob/ob mice (body weight fell by 30% after two weeks). They lack the hormone but have the receptor; db/db mice lack a working leptin receptor, so these injections did not reduce their body weight.
cards.quote: Leptin reduced their body weight by 30% after two weeks, and did not reduce the weight of db/db mice
cards.section: Evidence for a hormone: leptin

cards.front: A newly found obese mouse strain makes abundant, biologically active leptin but cannot respond to it. Predict the result of joining it to a normal mouse by parabiosis, and the likely class of defect.
cards.back: By Coleman's db/db logic, the mutant should keep eating while the normal partner eats less (the db/db partner starved). The likely defect is in the leptin receptor or its signalling.
cards.why: Rests on Coleman's logic: making plenty of the factor but not responding to it is the db pattern.
cards.quote: Yet the db/db mouse itself kept eating, so it cannot respond.
cards.section: Evidence for a hormone: joined mice

cards.front: Channelrhodopsin was expressed in arcuate AgRP neurons and excited with light trains in well-fed mice, which began eating. What kind of conclusion does this support?
cards.back: Sufficiency: imposed AgRP activity is enough to evoke feeding in well-fed mice, at least for that stimulation pattern.
cards.quote: This was sufficient to evoke feeding in well-fed mice, at least for that pattern.
cards.section: Testing the circuit: enough, needed, and when

cards.front: Ay mice overexpress agouti protein, which blocks melanocortin receptors, so their MC4R is already blocked. If AgRP neurons drove feeding only by blocking MC4R, what should optogenetic AgRP stimulation do in these mice? What was found?
cards.back: Prediction: no added feeding, since the receptors are already blocked. Found: stimulation still evoked feeding. So AgRP neurons have another route; they also release GABA and NPY.
cards.quote: In fact it still evoked feeding in Ay mice (Aponte and colleagues, 2011).
cards.section: Testing the circuit: enough, needed, and when

cards.front: AgRP neurons were killed with diphtheria toxin in adult mice and in newborn mice. What happened, and what does each result show?
cards.back: Adults rapidly starved: the cells are necessary for feeding in adults. Newborns showed minimal effects on feeding, suggesting developing circuits compensate.
cards.quote: Ablation in newborn mice had minimal effects on feeding, which suggests that developing circuits compensate.
cards.section: Testing the circuit: enough, needed, and when

cards.front: A hungry mouse has its AgRP neurons monitored by fibre photometry (calcium indicator fluorescence). A food cue appears but no food has yet been eaten. Predict the AgRP signal.
cards.back: It falls within seconds, before any eating begins. The hunger circuit reacts to signs of food, not only to food eaten.
cards.why: Gut nutrients act over minutes and leptin over hours, so this fast drop is driven by the cue.
cards.quote: AgRP activity, high in a hungry mouse, falls within seconds when food or a food cue appears, before eating begins
cards.section: Testing the circuit: enough, needed, and when

cards.front: AgRP activity drops within seconds of a food cue, before eating starts, yet AgRP neurons drive feeding. Which mouse result reconciles these, and how?
cards.back: Brief AgRP stimulation that ended before food arrived still increased later eating, so prior activity can leave a lasting drive even after the imposed stimulation ends. This helps explain how food-cue suppression can precede eating, without establishing that all AgRP activity during the meal is dispensable.
cards.quote: Brief AgRP stimulation that ended before food arrived still increased later eating
cards.section: Testing the circuit: enough, needed, and when

cards.front: For arcuate AgRP neurons, give one recording, one stimulation and one ablation result, and the kind of conclusion each supports.
cards.back: Recording: photometry activity falls at a food cue (correlation). Stimulation: channelrhodopsin excitation evokes eating in fed mice (sufficiency). Ablation: diphtheria toxin in adults causes starvation (necessity).
cards.quote: Ablation asks whether the cells are needed.
cards.section: Testing the circuit: enough, needed, and when

cards.front: MC4R activation opposes feeding, and human MC4R mutations are the most common single-gene cause of severe early-onset obesity. Prolonged POMC stimulation reduced intake through melanocortin signalling. As hypotheses to test, what would you predict for feeding and weight in a mouse lacking functional MC4R, and for the effect of prolonged POMC stimulation there?
cards.back: Hypotheses, not established results: the 'stop button' is gone, so the mouse overeats and becomes obese, as in people with MC4R mutations. Prolonged POMC stimulation should then fail to reduce intake, if its effect runs through MC4R (the lesson shows only that it needs melanocortin signalling).
cards.quote: Prolonged POMC stimulation reduced intake, and that effect required melanocortin signalling.
cards.section: Testing the circuit: enough, needed, and when

cards.front: Where are the midbrain dopamine neurons, and where do they project?
cards.back: Ventral tegmental area (VTA) and substantia nigra; they project to the striatum (including the nucleus accumbens) and to frontal cortex.
cards.quote: Dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and substantia nigra of the midbrain project to the striatum
cards.section: Dopamine neurons report prediction errors

cards.front: About three quarters of dopamine neurons recorded in two monkeys burst when juice arrived with no warning. In these responsive recordings, where did the burst occur once the monkeys learned that a sound predicted the juice?
cards.back: The burst came at the sound rather than at the juice.
cards.quote: Once the monkeys learned that a sound predicted the juice, the burst came at the sound rather than at the juice
cards.section: The recordings

cards.front: Dopamine-neuron recordings fit a reward prediction error. What can such recordings alone not show?
cards.back: That the signal teaches (recording shows only correlation), or anything about pleasure.
cards.why: The rule also covers only the quick responses of many, not all, dopamine neurons in tasks with predictable reward timing.
cards.quote: a recording alone does not show that the signal teaches, and the rule says nothing about pleasure
cards.section: The recordings

cards.front: In the Rescorla-Wagner rule, δ = r − V and V(next trial) = {{c1::V + α × δ}}, where α (0 to 1) is the learning rate.
cards.back: V is the cue's learned value, r the reward (1 for juice, 0 for none), δ the error.
cards.quote: In symbols: δ = r − V V(next trial) = V + α × δ
cards.section: A rule for learning from errors

cards.front: Rescorla-Wagner rule: α = 0.20, a reward r = 1 on every trial, and V = 0 at the start. Find V after trials 1 and 2, and δ on trial 3.
cards.quote: Here V is the cue's learned value, r the reward that arrives (1 for juice, 0 for none), δ the error
cards.section: A rule for learning from errors

cards.front: Rescorla-Wagner rule with r = 1 every trial and V = 0 at the start: the error shrinks by a factor of 1 − α each trial. With α = 0.5, what is V after four trials?
cards.quote: The error shrinks by the same factor, 1 − α = 0.7, on every trial.
cards.section: A rule for learning from errors

cards.front: Rescorla-Wagner rule: after training, a cue's value is V = 0.8. The reward is then omitted. What is δ? What is δ if instead a reward arrives with no cue (V = 0)?
cards.back: Omitted: δ = 0 − 0.8 = −0.8, a negative error at the expected time. Unpredicted reward: δ = 1 − 0 = +1.
cards.quote: omit the reward, and δ = 0 − 0.95 = −0.95, a negative error at the expected time
cards.section: A rule for learning from errors

cards.front: Why can the Rescorla-Wagner rule not produce the dopamine burst at a predictive cue?
cards.back: It updates the cue's value from trial to trial but has no time within a trial, so it cannot produce an error at the moment of the cue.
cards.quote: The Rescorla-Wagner rule updates the cue's value from trial to trial but has no time within a trial
cards.section: From the reward to the cue

cards.front: In the lesson's simplified temporal-difference (TD) model with discount factor 1, the TD error at each step is δ = r + {{c1::V(next moment) − V(this moment)}}: the reward in that step plus the change in prediction.
cards.quote: the reward that arrived in that step, plus the change in the prediction
cards.section: From the reward to the cue

cards.front: In the lesson's simplified TD model (γ = 1, tone at unpredictable times, V = 0 before the tone, V = 1 from tone to juice, V = 0 after juice), why is there a burst at the tone but none at the juice in a trained trial?
cards.back: At the tone the prediction jumps from 0 to 1 with no reward: δ = 0 + 1 − 0 = +1. At the juice r = 1 but the prediction falls from 1 to 0: δ = 1 + 0 − 1 = 0.
cards.why: Unexpected good news about future reward produces an error just as reward itself does.
cards.quote: unexpected good news about the future produces an error just as reward itself does
cards.section: From the reward to the cue

cards.front: A monkey is fully trained that a tone (at unpredictable times) is followed by juice 1 s later. On one trial the tone sounds but juice is withheld. Using the TD rule, predict δ and the dopamine response at the tone and at the time juice was due.
cards.back: Tone: δ = +1, a burst. Juice time: no reward, but the prediction drops from 1 to 0, so δ = 0 + 0 − 1 = −1, a pause exactly when juice was due.
cards.quote: At the juice time no reward arrives, yet the prediction still drops from 1 to 0
cards.section: From the reward to the cue

cards.front: In the TD model, a light at unpredictable times always comes 2 s before a tone, which comes 1 s before juice. After full training the burst is at the light. On a probe trial the tone sounds with no light before it, and juice follows. Predict the bursts.
cards.back: A burst at the tone and none at the juice. Without the light the tone is unpredicted, so the prediction jumps 0 to 1 there; the juice is predicted by the tone.
cards.why: Rule: the burst goes to the earliest cue that predicts reward without itself being predicted.
cards.quote: That is why, with learning, the burst moves to the earliest cue that predicts the reward without itself being predicted.
cards.section: From the reward to the cue

cards.front: In the TD model after learning (γ = 1, tone at unpredictable times, zero waiting baseline, average V = 0.25 after the tone, terminal V = 0), a tone predicts juice (r = 1) on only 25% of trials. In model units, what is δ at the tone, at the juice when it comes, and at the juice time when it does not?
cards.back: Prediction after the tone is about 0.25. Tone: +0.25. Juice delivered: 1 + 0 − 0.25 = +0.75. Juice omitted: 0 + 0 − 0.25 = −0.25.
cards.why: Real firing need not scale by the same fractions as model units.
cards.quote: Suppose the tone predicts juice on only half the trials.
cards.section: From the reward to the cue

cards.front: Monkeys learn cues that predict juice with different probabilities. How does the TD rule say dopamine responses at the cue and at the juice should change as probability rises, and what was found?
cards.back: Model: the cue error grows with probability p, the error at delivered juice (1 − p) shrinks. Found the same direction: cue responses grew with reward probability, reward responses shrank.
cards.why: An uncertain reward leaves some error at the reward even after learning.
cards.quote: responses to the cue grew with the probability of reward, and responses to the reward itself shrank
cards.section: From the reward to the cue

cards.front: In the TD model (γ = 1, zero waiting baseline), the body's state sets the size of the reward r. A monkey trained with juice worth r = 1 (V = 1 from tone to juice) is suddenly sated so the juice is worth r = 0.5. On the first such trial, holding learned predictions fixed and changing only r, what is δ at the tone and at the juice?
cards.back: Tone: δ = 0 + 1 − 0 = +1 (the learned prediction has not changed yet). Juice: δ = 0.5 + 0 − 1 = −0.5, a negative error.
cards.why: Rests on the modelling statement that hunger and satiety change r, plus the TD rule. Behaviour, not the recordings, supports that statement.
cards.quote: in the rules below, the body's state changes the size of the reward, r
cards.section: Two questions, one idea

cards.front: What is blocking, and why does a prediction-error rule explain it?
cards.back: A new cue added alongside a cue that already predicts reward is learned poorly. The reward is already predicted, so δ is about 0 and there is no error to drive learning about the new cue.
cards.quote: One known effect helps, blocking: a new cue added alongside one that already predicts reward is learned poorly, because the reward brings no error.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Design an experiment in rats testing whether an imposed dopamine burst is sufficient to make an animal learn about a cue it would otherwise ignore.
cards.back: Train cue A to predict reward; then reward A plus new cue X (X is normally blocked). In TH-Cre rats with Cre-dependent channelrhodopsin in the VTA, deliver light at reward on A plus X trials. First verify the construct is expressed mainly in dopamine neurons, since tyrosine hydroxylase is also made by noradrenaline cells. Test X alone: if X gains value, this imposed burst was sufficient in these rats.
cards.why: Controls: no-opsin rats given light; stimulation unpaired with reward; probe of X without stimulation. Steinberg and colleagues (2013) reported such unblocking.
cards.quote: Deliver light at the time of reward on the A plus X trials.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Optogenetic unblocking shows an imposed dopamine burst can be sufficient for learning. What experiment would show that natural bursts are necessary?
cards.back: Silence dopamine neurons at an unexpected reward, when a natural burst would occur, and show that learning then fails.
cards.quote: that requires silencing dopamine neurons at an unexpected reward, when a natural burst would occur, and showing that learning then fails
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Define wanting (incentive salience) and liking.
cards.back: Wanting: the motivational pull of a reward and its cues. Liking: the hedonic impact of the reward itself.
cards.quote: Wanting, or incentive salience, is the motivational pull of a reward and its cues.
cards.section: Wanting is not liking

cards.front: How is liking measured in animals without asking them?
cards.back: Taste reactivity: tongue protrusions to sweet, gapes to bitter, scored from video.
cards.quote: Liking can be measured in animals without asking, through taste reactivity
cards.section: Wanting is not liking

cards.front: Mice with dopamine transporter (DAT) expression at about 10% of normal reach sweet food sooner in a runway. Is that because they run faster?
cards.back: No. They paused less on the way; their running speed did not differ. They have about 70% more extracellular striatal dopamine.
cards.quote: They reached sweet food sooner in a runway because they paused less on the way; their running speed itself did not differ.
cards.section: Wanting is not liking

cards.front: Mice with the transporter DAT at about 10% of normal have a lifelong rise in extracellular striatal dopamine. Based on the DAT-knockdown and dopamine-depletion results, predict their approach to sweet food and their taste-reactivity responses to sucrose.
cards.back: They reached sweet food sooner because they paused less on the way (running speed itself did not differ), with no increase in liking reactions to sucrose. In these tests dopamine moved wanting, not liking.
cards.why: Caveat: the evidence comes from a lifelong mutation, which is not an acute or generic dopamine manipulation.
cards.quote: They showed no increase in liking reactions to sucrose (Peciña and colleagues, 2003).
cards.section: Wanting is not liking

cards.front: Dopamine depletion and DAT knockdown change wanting but not liking. Why does this not show that the quick dopamine burst is wanting?
cards.back: Both manipulations change dopamine for hours or a lifetime, not only its quick bursts. They show dopamine matters for wanting; how the error signal relates to incentive salience is open.
cards.quote: Both manipulations change dopamine for hours or a lifetime, not only its quick bursts
cards.section: Wanting is not liking

cards.front: Name two ways addictive drugs act on the dopamine transporter (DAT) to raise dopamine signalling.
cards.back: Blocking DAT, so released dopamine is not pumped back into the cell, or making DAT run in reverse, pushing dopamine out.
cards.quote: such as blocking DAT or making it run in reverse, pushing dopamine out
cards.section: In addiction, wanting can grow while liking does not

cards.front: What does incentive-sensitization theory propose about addiction?
cards.back: In susceptible individuals, repeated drug use makes incentive-salience circuits hypersensitive, so drug wanting, especially when triggered by cues, can grow out of proportion to drug liking. It offers an explanation for craving after the drug stops being enjoyable.
cards.why: It is a theory; habit learning, weakened prefrontal control, withdrawal and stress systems, genes and environment also matter.
cards.quote: so drug wanting, especially when triggered by cues, can grow out of proportion to drug liking
cards.section: In addiction, wanting can grow while liking does not

cards.front: In rats, ventromedial hypothalamic lesions caused overeating and obesity, and lateral hypothalamic lesions stopped eating. Why do these results not establish 'feeding centres'?
cards.back: The lesions destroyed everything in one place, including fibres passing through, so they showed where damage changed feeding, not what the cells there compute.
cards.quote: These early lesions destroyed everything in one place, including fibres passing through
cards.section: Feeding centres before the hormone

cards.front: In the full TD rule with discount factor γ = 0.9 per time step and five time steps between cue and reward, how large is the cue burst relative to a full burst?
cards.back: γ⁵ = 0.9⁵ ≈ 0.59 of a full burst. Longer cue-reward delays predict smaller cue responses.
cards.quote: Discounting shrinks the cue burst when the reward is far off.
cards.section: The full temporal-difference rule

cards.front: Illustrative mapping: resting rate 5 spikes/s, gain 20 spikes/s per unit of error, and firing cannot go below zero. Predict firing for δ = +0.5, −0.2 and −0.6.
cards.back: +0.5: 5 + 10 = 15 spikes/s. −0.2: 5 − 4 = 1 spike/s. −0.6: 5 − 12 = −7, so 0 spikes/s. Every δ of −0.25 or below gives zero: pauses saturate, bursts keep growing.
cards.quote: A firing rate cannot go below zero, so in this mapping every error of −0.25 or below gives the same zero firing
cards.section: Why a pause has less room than a burst
